families.body: The group looks strong, but it is two different stories. The established, profitable giants rose calmly. Quantum and AI funds rose twice as fast with three times the swings — same group, completely different ride.

learn.a: A basket of company shares that you buy in one go, like buying a single share. Buy one unit of an energy ETF and you own a slice of two hundred energy companies at once. You never pick the companies yourself — the fund follows a published list.
learn.b: That is why this app tracks funds instead of individual companies: one number stands for a whole idea.

learn.q: What is a ticker, like XLE or GDX?
learn.a: A short nickname the stock exchange gives every fund, three to four letters. The letters usually mean nothing useful — XLE is an energy fund, GDX holds gold miners, QTUM holds quantum computing companies. You type the ticker into your broker to find the fund.
learn.b: Two funds can hold nearly the same thing under different tickers. SMH and SOXX are both chip funds — different provider, slightly different list, different fee.

learn.q: What does the fee cost me in real money?
learn.a: Fees are quoted per year as a percentage. 0.50% a year on 1,000 is 5 a year. On 10,000 it is 50 a year. You never get a bill — it is quietly taken out of the fund price every day, which is why people forget it exists.
learn.b: It runs whether the fund goes up or down. Over ten years a 0.70% fund costs roughly seven times what a 0.10% fund costs on the same money.

learn.q: Why do theme funds cost more than broad ones?
learn.a: A broad fund holds whatever is biggest and barely changes — that is cheap to run, usually 0.03% to 0.10%. A theme fund has to decide what counts as “quantum computing”, then rebuild the list as companies come and go. That work is charged to you, usually 0.35% to 0.80%.
learn.b: Newer and narrower almost always means more expensive. Check the fee before the performance — the fee is the one number you know in advance.

learn.q: What is normal for each group here?
learn.a: Fees vary more by group than most people expect, because some groups have broad cheap funds available and some only have niche ones.
learn.b: The table below this card shows the average for all six groups, cheapest to most expensive.

learn.q: Why look at the top holdings?
learn.a: Because a “theme” can be one or two companies wearing a costume. Open the nuclear theme and Cameco alone is 22% of it. Open oil and Exxon plus Chevron are nearly 40%. If those two have a bad week, the whole theme has a bad week.
learn.b: A theme where the biggest holding is 5% behaves like a group of companies. One where it is 20% behaves like a bet on that company.

learn.a: It is how far prices swing around day to day, quoted as a yearly percentage. A calm fund at 11% mostly drifts. A wild one at 26% can be down 15% in a month and back up the next, with no news you would recognise.
learn.b: Same average return, very different experience. Bumpiness is the part people underestimate until they own it.

learn.q: If something is at its record high, is that good or bad?
learn.a: Both, and nobody knows which in advance. Records happen in strong markets, so a fund at its high is often doing genuinely well. It is also the price at which every previous buyer is happy and the next buyer has the least cushion.
learn.b: This app flags it rather than judging it. When a theme is at its high the score looks great, which is exactly when the score is least useful on its own.

learn.a: If the companies inside pay dividends, the fund receives them. Some funds pass the cash to you a few times a year; others quietly buy more shares with it, so it shows up as a higher price instead. The fund name usually says: distributing pays out, accumulating reinvests.
learn.b: All the numbers in this app assume dividends are included — otherwise energy and banks would look far worse than they are.

learn.a: Daily prices are mostly noise. A month is long enough that a real change shows up and short enough to notice. The scores are built from every daily close, then published once a month, so nothing is thrown away but nothing is over-read either.
learn.b: A weather forecast is the honest comparison: useful, directional, and wrong sometimes.
